newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Apathetic Europe pressured on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Apathetic Europe pressured on Zaire.

text.p: Europe, virtually paralysed by indifference, came under renewed pressure on Tuesday to act to help more than one million refugees in eastern Zaire, the victims of central Africa's latest bout of bloodletting.

France, pushing for some form of multinational force to ensure security for food aid deliveries, said it was receiving a favourable response to its proposal to help people caught by fighting between Zairean troops and Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels.

But behind pious declarations on the need for action to deal with Africa's latest humanitarian crisis, diplomats said most of France's European Union partners had no intention of becoming involved, particularly militarily.
"France can of course do what it likes, but no-one else has the slightest intention of doing anything like that (military intervention)," said one EU diplomat.

Meanwhile, the problems of any international action in the Great Lakes region were underlined on Tuesday when Rwanda said it would strongly oppose an international presence "by all means, not only political".

The message, delivered at a Brussels press conference by Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana, reflected Kigali's deep distrust of France, a long-time supporter of former Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana.
Habyarimana's death in 1994 triggered a genocide by Hutu hardliners of around one million mainly Tutsi Rwandans.

That genocide ended with the current Tutsi-led government's victory, but a belated humanitarian intervention led by France gave many of the Hutu killers an effective sanctuary in eastern Zaire where they evaded arrest and plotted a comeback.
The European Union's aid chief Emma Bonino called on Tuesday for a ceasefire in the area to allow aid corridors to the refugees to be opened.

In several newspaper interviews, Bonino said African countries in the region would have to give some clear undertaking the fighting was over in order to allow a European humanitarian operation to start.
Relief workers as well as refugees needed protection, as they could come under attack from starving mobs who had not had any food for a week, she said.
Aid workers and regional analysts said the EU countries, including France, had not even tried to address the problem of how to end insecurity in the region.

EU sources said a meeting of experts in Brussels on Tuesday would discuss possible "safe corridor" routes and food aid deliveries ahead of a meeting of cooperation and development ministers on Thursday.
Hopes of any form of serious regional initiative to end the crisis dimmed further on Tuesday when Zaire stayed away from a summit of east and central African countries.
French President Jacques Chirac said his proposed force was crucial to help ensure that aid got through to the refugees, the whereabouts of many of whom are now a mystery.
Fearful of returning to Rwanda, many are believed to have scattered in small groups deep into the heart of Zaire.

Chirac, who wants an international cloak for any French action, said the force should include soldiers "from all major nations, particularly the United States". He said it must first be approved by the United Nations Security Council after which Africans should rapidly take over.

"We have suggested sending a force to ensure security... which should be decided upon by the Security Council and could as soon as possible be replaced by an African force with U.S. and European backing," Chirac told a news conference.
Aid workers and regional diplomats dismiss talk of an African force as simple time-wasting.
"It is window-dressing, it would take so long to organise it is simply fanciful," said one regional diplomat.
